subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 49-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show AST 180 U/L and ALT 75 U/L, with an elevated total bilirubin.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected aminotransferase pattern in this patient?

options.text: ALT > AST with levels above 1000 U/L, suggesting acute viral hepatitis
AST > ALT with a ratio greater than 2:1, and AST typically not exceeding 500 U/L in alcoholic hepatitis
ALT > AST with a ratio greater than 2:1, as in most nonalcoholic liver disease
Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation with normal aminotransferases
AST > ALT with levels above 1000 U/L, indicating acetaminophen toxicity

explanation_correct: In alcoholic liver disease, AST exceeds ALT, usually with a ratio greater than 2:1 (make a toast with alcohol). In alcoholic hepatitis, AST does not typically exceed 500 U/L. In most other liver diseases ALT > AST, and AST > ALT in nonalcoholic disease suggests progression to advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis. Aminotransferases above 1000 U/L point instead to drug-induced liver injury such as acetaminophen toxicity, ischemic hepatitis, acute viral hepatitis, or autoimmune hepatitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: ALT > AST is typical of most liver disease, but values above 1000 U/L suggest acetaminophen, ischemic, or acute viral hepatitis rather than alcoholic hepatitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: ALT > AST is the general rule in nonalcoholic liver disease; this patient's reversed pattern with a heavy alcohol history points to alcohol.
explanation_incorrect.D: An isolated alkaline phosphatase rise with normal transaminases suggests cholestasis, biliary obstruction, or infiltrative disease rather than alcoholic hepatitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: AST > ALT with values above 1000 U/L suggests acetaminophen toxicity or ischemic hepatitis; alcoholic hepatitis usually remains below 500 U/L.

educationalObjective: Alcoholic liver disease shows AST > ALT (usually >2:1) with AST below 500 U/L in alcoholic hepatitis; levels above 1000 U/L suggest other causes.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 63-year-old woman has fatigue and pruritus. Laboratory testing shows an elevated alkaline phosphatase. A bone scan is negative, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase is also elevated.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Paget disease of bone, because GGT rises in bone disease
Acute viral hepatitis, because ALP and GGT are hepatocellular enzymes
Cholestatic or biliary disease, because GGT rises in liver and biliary disease but not bone disease
Hemolysis, because both enzymes are released from erythrocytes
Advanced cirrhosis, because GGT replaces albumin as a synthetic marker

explanation_correct: Alkaline phosphatase is elevated in cholestasis (eg, biliary obstruction), infiltrative disorders, and bone disease. Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase is located on the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes like ALP and rises in various liver and biliary diseases but not in bone disease; it is also associated with alcohol use. A parallel rise in ALP and GGT therefore localizes the process to the liver or biliary tree rather than bone.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bone disease raises ALP but not GGT, so an elevated GGT argues against a primary bone disorder such as Paget disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Acute viral hepatitis predominantly raises ALT and AST, often above 1000 U/L, rather than producing an isolated ALP and GGT pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, not alkaline phosphatase or GGT.
explanation_incorrect.E: GGT is not a marker of synthetic function; albumin, prothrombin time, and platelets reflect biosynthetic function in advanced disease.

educationalObjective: GGT parallels ALP in hepatobiliary disease but is normal in bone disease, helping localize an elevated alkaline phosphatase.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain 2 days after an intentional overdose. Laboratory studies show AST 3200 U/L, ALT 2800 U/L, and an elevated bilirubin.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this degree of aminotransferase elevation?

options.text: Alcoholic hepatitis
Chronic autoimmune hepatitis with established cirrhosis
Hepatic steatosis from metabolic dysfunction
Drug-induced liver injury (acetaminophen toxicity)
Alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension

explanation_correct: Aminotransferases above 1000 U/L have a limited differential: drug-induced liver injury (eg, acetaminophen toxicity), ischemic hepatitis, acute viral hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. This patient's acute presentation after an overdose with AST and ALT in the thousands fits acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. Alcoholic hepatitis typically keeps AST below 500 U/L, while chronic stable cirrhosis and simple steatosis produce only modest enzyme elevations.

explanation_incorrect.A: Alcoholic hepatitis gives AST > ALT but AST does not typically exceed 500 U/L.
explanation_incorrect.B: Autoimmune hepatitis can enter the differential for marked transaminase elevation, but the acute overdose context and established cirrhosis make acetaminophen far more likely.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatosis usually causes mild ALT and AST elevations, not values in the thousands.
explanation_incorrect.E: Alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension produces only moderate enzyme rises along with findings such as thrombocytopenia and varices.

educationalObjective: Aminotransferases above 1000 U/L suggest acetaminophen toxicity, ischemic hepatitis, acute viral hepatitis, or autoimmune hepatitis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 58-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis is evaluated for worsening ascites. Laboratory studies show hypoalbuminemia, a prolonged prothrombin time, and thrombocytopenia.
question: Which of the following best accounts for these laboratory abnormalities?

options.text: Increased hepatic synthesis of albumin and clotting factors due to regeneration
Enhanced platelet clearance by the liver due to increased thrombopoietin
Acute cholestasis causing reduced bilirubin conjugation
Portal hypertension alone causing all three abnormalities, independent of synthetic function
Decreased hepatic synthesis of albumin and clotting factors and thrombopoietin, plus splenic sequestration from portal hypertension

explanation_correct: Albumin falls in advanced liver disease as a marker of the liver's biosynthetic function. Prothrombin time rises because of reduced production of clotting factors. Platelets fall from decreased thrombopoietin production and hepatic sequestration, and portal hypertension adds splenomegaly with splenic sequestration. Hyperbilirubinemia can accompany liver disease but is not itself a synthetic-function marker.

explanation_incorrect.A: Advanced liver disease reduces rather than increases synthesis of albumin and clotting factors despite the presence of regenerative nodules.
explanation_incorrect.B: Thrombopoietin production falls in advanced liver disease rather than rising, and platelets are sequestered rather than actively cleared.
explanation_incorrect.C: Altered bilirubin metabolism does not explain hypoalbuminemia, a prolonged prothrombin time, or thrombocytopenia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Portal hypertension contributes to thrombocytopenia through splenic sequestration, but low albumin and a prolonged prothrombin time reflect lost synthetic function.

educationalObjective: Low albumin, prolonged PT, and low platelets are the classic laboratory triad of advanced liver disease and impaired hepatic synthetic function.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 30-year-old woman presents with fatigue and jaundice. Serologies confirm acute hepatitis B. Her aminotransferases are elevated with ALT greater than AST.
question: Which of the following statements about this laboratory pattern is correct?

options.text: ALT > AST is the typical pattern in most liver diseases
AST > ALT with a ratio greater than 2:1 is expected in all forms of hepatitis
ALT > AST occurs only in alcoholic liver disease
Such elevations always exceed 1000 U/L in acute viral hepatitis
This pattern specifically indicates advanced fibrosis rather than acute injury

explanation_correct: In most liver diseases ALT exceeds AST. Alcoholic liver disease is the classic exception with AST > ALT, usually greater than 2:1. Very high aminotransferases above 1000 U/L occur in acute viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, ischemic hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis, but not every case is that high. Persistent AST > ALT in nonalcoholic liver disease, not ALT > AST, suggests progression to advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: An AST > ALT ratio greater than 2:1 is characteristic of alcoholic liver disease, not all forms of hepatitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alcoholic liver disease is the classic cause of AST > ALT, the reverse of this patient's pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Not every acute viral hepatitis exceeds 1000 U/L; that degree of elevation also suggests acetaminophen toxicity, ischemia, or autoimmune hepatitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: It is AST > ALT in nonalcoholic liver disease that suggests advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, not ALT > AST.

educationalObjective: ALT > AST is the usual pattern in most liver disease; AST > ALT suggests alcohol use or advanced fibrosis.
